title: Can you structure these 17 profitability and revenue decline questions in two minutes each?
description: 17 profitability and revenue decline case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, if you make the profit split automatic: profit = revenue − costs, revenue = volume × price, and then segment by product, customer or channel until you find where the money went. Profitability and revenue decline cases are the most common type you will meet. Here are 17 prompts, from ski resorts to grocers: two minutes each, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. Start with one question: is this the whole market or just our client? Then split the metric the client cares about into its drivers in the client's own terms (occupancy × rate for a hotel, covers × spend for a restaurant) and say where you would start. The model gives the buckets, the starting point and the trap. For the full method, see the profitability framework.

1. A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show a model structure
  • Market: rates, house prices and transactions; is everyone down 20%?
  • Our offer: rates and fees versus rivals; loan-to-value limits.
  • Channels: are brokers placing less with us; online and branch conversion.
  • Process: time to decision and approval rate; drop-off during the application.

Start: the market. If every bank is down 20%, it is not ours to fix. Trap: marketing ideas before checking the market.

2. A ski resort's profits fell 40% after two warm winters.

Show a model structure
  • Winter revenue: visitors × spend by month; lift passes, ski school, food, rentals.
  • Costs: fixed (lifts, staff, maintenance); snow-related (snowmaking, energy).
  • Snow risk: days open, altitude, snowmaking coverage; trend or bad luck?
  • Non-ski income: summer, events and conferences.

Start: days open. Warm winters shorten the season while most costs stay fixed. Trap: treating it as a normal decline and missing the weather.

3. A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show a model structure
  • Doctors: awareness and trust in the data; specialists versus family doctors.
  • Patients: how many are diagnosed and eligible (was the forecast realistic?); side effects and stopping early.
  • Payers: reimbursement approval; restrictions such as "only after other drugs fail".
  • Competition: rival drugs and generics; their pricing.

Start: payers. If insurers restrict it, doctors and patients can do little. Trap: assuming it is a marketing problem.

4. A cinema chain's attendance is still 25% below pre-pandemic levels.

Show a model structure
  • Market: total attendance versus ours; supply of big releases.
  • Our offer: ticket and snack prices; comfort, screens and locations.
  • Substitutes: shorter streaming windows; home viewing habits.
  • Customers: which groups have not come back; frequency versus number of visitors.

Start: are we below the industry, or is the whole market smaller? Trap: ignoring the film slate, which drives much of attendance.

5. A software company's customer churn has doubled to 2% a month.

Show a model structure
  • Who leaves: size, plan and account age.
  • Why: product gaps, bugs, a price rise; a competitor or no longer needed.
  • When: after onboarding, at renewal, after a release.
  • Response: onboarding and support; contracts and customer success.

Start: who is leaving. Churn is rarely spread evenly. Trap: retention discounts before knowing who leaves and why.

6. A grocer's operating margin fell from 4% to 2% in two years, while sales grew.

Show a model structure
  • Prices and mix: discounting to match rivals; shift to lower-margin categories.
  • Cost of goods: supplier prices, waste and shrinkage; private label share.
  • Store costs: wages, energy and rent as a share of sales.
  • Online: share of sales online; cost to pick and deliver each order.

Start: which cost grew faster than sales, measured as a percentage of sales. Trap: talking about growing sales when the problem is margin.

7. A city hotel's revenue per available room fell 15% this year.

Show a model structure
  • Occupancy: rooms sold versus available, by business, leisure and groups.
  • Room rate: average price versus rivals; discounting.
  • Market: city demand from events and offices; new hotels nearby.
  • Channels: ranking on booking sites; direct and corporate bookings.

Start: occupancy or rate, then which segment. Trap: treating revenue per room as one number.

8. A casual-dining chain's profit per restaurant has halved in three years.

Show a model structure
  • Covers: guests per week; lunch versus dinner, weekday versus weekend.
  • Spend per guest: prices, drinks and desserts; vouchers.
  • Food costs: ingredient prices and waste; mix towards low-margin dishes.
  • Restaurant costs: staff hours and wages; rent, energy, delivery fees.

Start: covers. Fewer guests spread fixed costs thinly. Trap: blaming food inflation without checking footfall.

9. A car dealer group's profit fell 30% even though it sold more cars.

Show a model structure
  • New cars: margin per car and maker bonuses; discounts to hit targets.
  • Used cars: volume, price and days in stock; stock bought at the peak.
  • Finance and insurance: share of buyers taking finance; commission per deal.
  • Service and parts: workshop hours sold.
  • Costs: interest on stock, staff and property.

Start: profit by business line. New cars usually carry thin margins for dealers; used cars, finance and servicing matter more. Trap: looking only at new-car volume.

10. A shopping app's conversion from visit to purchase fell from 4% to 3%.

Show a model structure
  • Traffic mix: new versus returning; ads, search and social.
  • Funnel step: product page, basket, checkout or payment.
  • Offer: prices, stock and delivery; rivals' promotions.
  • Technical: a new release, speed, payment errors.

Start: traffic mix. Cheap ads can bring visitors who were never going to buy. Trap: redesigning checkout before checking whether the visitors changed.

11. A car insurer's claims costs rose 25% in a year while customer numbers were flat.

Show a model structure
  • Number of claims: claims per 1,000 policies; accidents, theft, weather.
  • Cost per claim: parts and labour; hire cars and injury payouts.
  • Customer mix: younger drivers and riskier areas.
  • Fraud and process: suspicious claims; repair supplier contracts.

Start: frequency versus severity. Trap: raising prices for everyone before knowing which customers cost more.

12. A meal-kit company acquires plenty of customers but still loses money.

Show a model structure
  • Cost to acquire: marketing per new customer; first-box discounts.
  • How long they stay: churn after the discount ends; orders per customer.
  • Margin per box: ingredients and packaging; picking and delivery.
  • Fixed costs: kitchens, warehouses, head office.

Start: how long customers stay. If most leave after the discount, acquisition is wasted. Trap: celebrating customer growth.

13. A consulting firm's consultants billed 62% of their time this year, down from 75%.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: projects sold and pipeline.
  • Supply: hiring ahead of demand; fewer leavers than planned.
  • Matching: skills in the wrong place; gaps between projects.
  • Non-billable time: proposals, training; how time is recorded.

Start: did sales fall, or did headcount grow faster? Trap: cutting training before checking for over-hiring.

14. A gym chain loses 50% of new members within six months.

Show a model structure
  • When: first three months; when a promotional price ends.
  • Who: discount joiners, age, goals; visits in the first month.
  • Experience: crowding, cleanliness, classes; onboarding.
  • Price and contract: price versus rivals; ease of cancelling.

Start: visits in the first month. Members who do not build a habit leave. Trap: bigger joining discounts, which attract more people likely to leave.

15. A shampoo brand has lost 4 points of market share in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Where share went: which rivals or own-label; which channels.
  • Price: price gap; promotion frequency.
  • Product and brand: rival launches; advertising.
  • Distribution: shelf space and stock-outs; online visibility.

Start: who took the share. Losing to own-label suggests price; losing to a rival launch suggests product. Trap: more advertising first.

16. A dairy cooperative's margin fell from 8% to 3% while milk volumes grew.

Show a model structure
  • Milk price paid to farmers: per litre versus market; contract commitments.
  • Product mix: cheese, butter, liquid milk, powder.
  • Selling prices: supermarket contracts; export prices and currency.
  • Processing: energy, packaging, transport; plant utilisation.

Start: price paid versus price received. A co-op is squeezed between the two and may choose to pay its farmer-owners more. Trap: pushing volume, which adds more low-margin milk.

17. How can a car maker raise its operating margin from 4% to 8%?

Show a model structure
  • Price and mix: more premium models, fewer discounts; options.
  • Materials: shared platforms, fewer parts; supplier terms.
  • Manufacturing: plant utilisation and closures; automation.
  • Overheads: fewer models, focused R&D; sales costs.

Start: price and mix. Fewer discounts can add more margin than cost cuts. Trap: only cutting costs.

How to score your answer: make the tree add up

Take the ski resort. Suppose profit fell from $10M to $6M. The $4M drop must be explained by revenue and cost changes. If fewer skier days cut revenue by $3M and extra snowmaking added $1M of energy cost, the bridge is complete: $3M + $1M = $4M. Only then compare fixes such as flexible staffing, more snowmaking, advance pass sales and summer activities.

When you check your structure, ask whether the buckets could explain the number without gaps or overlaps, and whether your first data request was the most informative one.
